"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time. Running independent copies side by side, or splitting each single step across GPUs, does not count.
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"MCMC is serial: each likelihood evaluation waits on the previous one, and effective sample size grows as T/τ_int, where the autocorrelation time τ_int is fixed by posterior geometry (parameter correlation, equifinality, multimodality), not by hardware. For lumped rainfall-runoff models each step costs milliseconds, so the blocker is mixing, not per-step compute; more GPUs only run more of the same correlated chains and leave τ_int untouched.\",\"assumption\":\"The posterior must be approximated by a Markov chain built from scratch for each catchment, and the only way to spend compute is more steps or more chains.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the unit of work from chain steps to independent simulator runs: amortized simulation-based inference. Draw parameters from a proposal, run the model in massively parallel GPU batches, and train a neural posterior estimator once (ideally across hundreds of catchments). Inference for any basin is then one forward pass, and every extra GPU-hour lowers posterior error instead of adding correlated samples.\",\"question\":\"For a benchmark set (e.g., 10 CAMELS basins with a GR4J-type model), how many simulations N does neural posterior estimation need before the C2ST classifier accuracy between NPE posterior samples and a 1e6-step DREAM reference posterior falls below 0.55 (chance level)?\",\"measure\":\"Run one long DREAM reference chain per basin (1e5–1e6 evaluations at ~5–50 ms each: a few CPU-hours), then generate N = 1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6 parallel simulations (minutes on one GPU), train the estimator (~1 GPU-hour), and record C2ST and MMD versus the reference as a function of N. Rough cost: about 1 GPU-day plus 1 CPU-day total.\",\"compute_after\":\"Each additional GPU-hour raises N and directly reduces posterior approximation error with near-linear parallel scaling; amortized across catchments, the marginal cost of calibrating a new basin approaches zero.\",\"exact\":\"Success = C2ST < 0.55 and posterior-predictive NSE within 0.01 of the MCMC reference at N ≤ 1e5 simulations for at least 8 of 10 basins.\",\"expected\":\"For a 6–10 parameter lumped model with a smooth likelihood, NPE reaches tolerance at N ≈ 1e4–1e5, i.e., minutes of GPU time versus days of serial MCMC, with the advantage compounding when one network serves many basins.\",\"fails_if\":\"Including error-model/observation-noise parameters makes the posterior sharply multimodal so C2ST stays above 0.55 even at N ≥ 1e6, or basins outside the training distribution require per-basin retraining that consumes the amortization gain.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Cranmer, Brehmer & Louppe 2020 (simulation-based inference review) and Lueckmann et al. 2017 (neural posterior estimation); DREAM(ZS) as the incumbent sampler (Vrugt et al. 2009); recent neural-density-estimation applications to conceptual hydrological models.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"The objective is the full joint parameter posterior, so every chain step pays for a full-record simulation and spends samples resolving equifinality ridges that barely move any decision-relevant prediction; the tail predictions that actually matter (flood design quantiles) converge slowest. Compute buys more samples of quantities nobody uses.\",\"assumption\":\"One must first estimate the entire parameter posterior and only afterwards propagate it to predictions; the quantity to be estimated is fixed as the posterior itself.\",\"reframe\":\"Change what is measured: target the decision quantity directly — e.g., the posterior of the 1%-exceedance (100-year) flood quantile — by emulating the map from parameters to that quantity with a Gaussian process, choosing evaluation points actively, and using importance weighting toward the tail. Compute is spent only where it changes the answer.\",\"question\":\"Does GP emulation with active point selection estimate the posterior mean and 95% interval of the 100-year flood quantile to within ±5% relative error using ≤1e3 model evaluations, where brute MCMC propagation needs ≥1e5, across 10 basins?\",\"measure\":\"On one basin, obtain ground truth from a long DREAM run propagated to the quantile (a few CPU-hours). Then run the active-learning GP at budgets of 250–2000 evaluations, repeat 10 times for variance, and record relative RMSE versus evaluation count. Rough cost: one laptop-weekend, about 2 CPU-days.\",\"compute_after\":\"Additional evaluations are placed where the functional is most uncertain or most tail-heavy, so added compute shrinks error on the decision quantity itself — including the rare tail where plain MCMC is weakest — rather than lengthening a chain.\",\"exact\":\"Success = relative error of the quantile's posterior mean and interval ≤5% with ≥90% confidence at ≤1e3 evaluations, i.e., at least 100x fewer evaluations than the MCMC reference.\",\"expected\":\"For smooth, low-dimensional functionals of a lumped model, expect a 10–100x reduction in required evaluations; the gain shrinks if the quantile is controlled by a wide, flat parameter region (strong predictive equifinality).\",\"fails_if\":\"The parameter-to-quantile map is discontinuous or oscillatory (threshold, snow, or switching processes), so emulation needs about as many points as MCMC, or stakeholders genuinely need the full joint posterior for multiple changing objectives.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Kandasamy et al. 2017 (Bayesian active learning for posterior estimation); GP and polynomial-chaos emulation of hydrological models (Reichert et al. 2011; Razavi et al. 2012 review); subset simulation for rare-event estimation (Au & Beck 2001).\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"Both per-step cost and chain length scale with the full continuous record: the model's state recursion forces a decades-long sequential simulation for every likelihood call, and the likelihood weights every timestep equally even though only a few percent of timesteps (storm events, recessions) constrain the parameters. The dependency over time is the part that waits, and it need not.\",\"assumption\":\"Calibration must run the model continuously over the whole record, and all timesteps are equally informative; cutting time necessarily biases inference.\",\"reframe\":\"Cut and reorder the unit of work: decompose the record into near-independent hydrologic events (with short warm-ups) plus recession blocks, calibrate each block in parallel, and combine the block posteriors (consensus Bayes), or use an event-only likelihood. The serial unit shrinks from decades to days, and blocks are embarrassingly parallel.\",\"question\":\"Per parameter: what fraction of posterior information (inverse posterior variance, or integrated parameter sensitivity) is carried by event and recession segments covering ≤10% of timesteps, and what is the Wasserstein-2 distance between the block-combined posterior and the full-record posterior, in units of posterior standard deviation?\",\"measure\":\"On one basin: compute per-timestep Jacobians of simulated flow with respect to parameters (one simulation plus adjoint or finite differences — minutes), aggregate information by segment type; then calibrate event-only and full-record posteriors (a few CPU-hours each) and compare W2 distance, coverage, and wall-clock per effective sample. Rough cost: 1–2 CPU-days.\",\"compute_after\":\"After the cut, more compute parallelizes across events, recessions, and basins simultaneously, and each likelihood call is a short recursion — GPUs reduce wall-clock directly instead of producing more correlated draws of a slow serial chain.\",\"exact\":\"Success = segments covering ≤10% of timesteps carry ≥90% of per-parameter information, AND the combined event posterior lies within W2 ≤ 0.1 posterior standard deviations of the full-record posterior, with a ≥10x reduction in serial simulation length per likelihood call.\",\"expected\":\"Quickflow, routing, and event-scale parameters are identified almost entirely from events; baseflow and water-balance parameters from recession and low-flow blocks — a two-block decomposition should retain nearly all information while cutting serial length 5–20x.\",\"fails_if\":\"A slow store (groundwater or snow) with memory longer than any block couples events across seasons, so block posteriors cannot be merged without bias and the full-record recursion is genuinely necessary.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Consensus and embarrassingly parallel MCMC (Scott et al. 2016; Neiswanger et al. 2014); hydrologic-signature and event-based calibration literature (McMillan et al. on signatures; limits-of-acceptability work); parallel-in-time integration methods as the general family.\"}]

Let me analyze each proposal.

**Proposal 1:**
- Bottleneck: MCMC is serial, autocorrelation time fixed by posterior geometry, more GPUs only run more correlated chains.
- Reframe: Change the unit of work from chain steps to independent simulator runs: amortized simulation-based inference. Draw parameters from proposal, run model in massively parallel GPU batches, train neural posterior estimator. Every extra GPU-hour lowers posterior approximation error instead of adding correlated samples.
- This changes what is computed: instead of Markov chain samples, they train a neural posterior estimator from independent runs. The MCMC chain step dependency is removed — simulator runs are independent, computed at the same time. More compute buys something it did not before (lower approximation error, amortization across catchments).
- Kind: reframe.
- Meets criterion: The criterion is about removing a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations, solver iterations) so that steps are computed at the same time. Here, MCMC chain steps are the serial dependency. By switching to NPE with independent simulator runs, the chain iteration dependency is removed — the runs are batched in parallel. Yes, it removes the chain-iteration dependency. Hmm, but the criterion says "removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time." In NPE, the simulator runs replace chain steps — they're independent, computed simultaneously. So yes, it meets the criterion. Actually wait — the question is whether the reframing removes such a dependency. The original bottleneck says "each likelihood evaluation waits on the previous one" — chain iterations. The reframe removes this by using independent simulator runs computed in parallel batches. So meets_criterion: yes.
- Quote: "Change the unit of work from chain steps to independent simulator runs: amortized simulation-based inference." Or "every extra GPU-hour lowers posterior approximation error instead of adding correlated samples."
- Reason: Replaces serial chain steps with independent parallel simulator runs; extra compute reduces posterior error.

**Proposal 2:**
- Bottleneck: every chain step pays for full-record simulation; samples resolve equifinality ridges that don't move decision-relevant predictions; tail predictions converge slowest.
- Reframe: Change what is measured: target the decision quantity directly (100-year flood quantile) via GP emulation with active point selection and importance weighting toward tail. Compute spent only where it changes the answer.
- Kind: reframe — changes what is measured (the decision quantity rather than the full joint posterior). More compute (active evaluations) buys accuracy on the decision quantity.
- Meets criterion: Does it remove a step-after-step dependency (time steps, chain iterations, solver iterations)? No — it changes the target of estimation and uses active learning, but there's no removal of a serial dependency. The active learning is sequential (choosing points adaptively), but that's not what the criterion asks. It doesn't remove chain iteration dependency so that steps are computed at the same time. Actually, it still may use MCMC-like sampling for the posterior of the quantile? It targets the decision quantity directly via emulation. The dependency structure isn't the focus. Meets_criterion: no.
- Quote: "Change what is measured: target the decision quantity directly — e.g., the posterior of the 1%-exceedance (100-year) flood quantile..."
- Reason: Changes the estimated quantity and evaluation strategy, not any serial step dependency; compute goes to tail accuracy.

**Proposal 3:**
- Bottleneck: the model's state recursion forces a decades-long sequential simulation for every likelihood call — the dependency over time is the part that waits.
- Reframe: Cut and reorder the unit of work: decompose record into near-independent hydrologic events plus recession blocks, calibrate each block in parallel, combine block posteriors (consensus Bayes). Serial unit shrinks from decades to days; blocks embarrassingly parallel.
- Kind: reframe — changes what is computed (unit of work cut into blocks) so more compute buys parallelism across events.
- Meets criterion: Does it remove a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps...)? Yes — the state recursion over time steps is the dependency; cutting the record into independent events removes the time-step dependency, so timesteps/blocks are computed at the same time. This is a clear yes: "The dependency over time is the part that waits, and it need not." It removes time-step dependency within the simulation. The criterion mentions "time steps" explicitly. Yes.
- Quote: "Cut and reorder the unit of work: decompose the record into near-independent hydrologic events (with short warm-ups) plus recession blocks, calibrate each block in parallel..."
- Reason: Removes time-step recursion dependency by splitting record into parallel independent event blocks.

Now, careful about criterion for proposal 1: The criterion says "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time." For proposal 1, the reframe replaces chain iterations with independent simulation runs — those weren't "steps computed at the same time" of the original chain; rather the whole chain is replaced. Hmm. The spirit: does the reframe eliminate a serial dependency so that the formerly sequential work becomes simultaneous? In proposal 1, the chain steps are eliminated, not parallelized — the new unit of work (independent simulator runs) is inherently parallel. The dependency is removed (there is no longer any waiting of one answer on the previous). I'd say yes: the chain iteration dependency that each likelihood evaluation waits on is removed, and the simulations are computed simultaneously. The criterion says "removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on... so that those steps are computed at the same time." In NPE, the simulator runs replace chain steps and are computed at the same time. I think yes is right.

Alternatively, one could argue "no" because the chain is replaced entirely rather than its steps being parallelized. But the criterion language "removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations...)" — proposal 1's bottleneck explicitly says "MCMC is serial: each likelihood evaluation waits on the previous one." The reframe removes that dependency by making runs independent and simultaneous. I'll say yes.

For proposal 3: clearly yes — "The dependency over time is the part that waits, and it need not." Time steps in the simulation are the dependency; blocks computed simultaneously.

For proposal 2: no serial dependency removal; it's about targeting the decision quantity. Meets_criterion: no.

Kinds: all three are reframes? Proposal 2 changes what is measured — that fits "reframe" definition ("changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before"). Yes, reframe. None are "copies" or "other."

Actually, let me reconsider. The distinction between "removing a dependency so steps run simultaneously" vs "replacing the algorithm with an embarrassingly parallel one." This is a judgment call. Let me think about what the criterion intends. The criterion is one specific property: eliminating a serial dependency so that formerly sequential steps become simultaneous. Let me think again about the exact wording: "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time."

Chain iterations: in MCMC, each state depends on the previous state. NPE removes this: parameter draws are independent and simulations run simultaneously. The posterior "answer" no longer waits on sequential chain iterations. The simulations — which serve the role of the chain's likelihood evaluations — are computed at the same time. Each MCMC step involved a likelihood evaluation (simulation); in NPE, those simulations are all done simultaneously. So the per-step work (simulations/likelihood evaluations) that was formerly chained is now done at once. That actually fits: the chain iterations each contained a simulation; NPE extracts the simulations from the chain and runs them all at once. So "those steps" (the simulation-containing steps) are computed at the same time, decoupled from the sequential dependency.

I'm fairly confident: proposal 1 meets_criterion = yes.

And proposal 3 clearly yes.

Proposal 2 clearly no.
